title: Sony’s New Flagship TV Lets You Tweak Its Settings Endlessly
gist: Wired gives Sony's flagship Bravia 9 II, an RGB LED/LCD TV Sony calls "True RGB", an 8/10. It is very bright, has no glare, has wide viewing angles and lets you tune black levels in detail. It costs $3,600 for 65 inches, $1,400 below LG's Micro RGB Evo, but it can't match OLED blacks (Samsung S95H) and is slightly less colorful than the LG.

insights.claim: Sony's flagship Bravia 9 II TV costs $3,600 for the 65-inch model, $1,400 less than the $5,000 LG Micro RGB Evo. Wired rated it 8/10 and placed it a notch or two below the best TVs available.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: The price ladder at the premium end of TVs shows Sony undercutting LG's RGB flagship rather than competing on absolute quality.
insights.quote: it’s just a notch or two lower than the absolute best television you might find

insights.claim: Wired's reviewer says a $3,600 flagship TV is worth it mainly to viewers of dark, cinematic content, since many TVs cost about $2,000 and work well out of the box for sports, animation and network TV.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Flagship TV demand depends on a niche cinematic use case. The mass market is satisfied around the $2,000 tier, which caps the premium-segment mix.
insights.quote: But is the Sony Bravia 9 II worth $3,600 when so many TVs cost around $2,000?
insights.locator: Knowing you can tweak the settings

insights.claim: RGB TVs like the Sony Bravia 9 II make color with red, green and blue LEDs shining through an LCD panel. Unlike OLED pixels, these lights cannot be switched off entirely, so the Bravia 9 II's blacks look less realistic than those of Samsung's S95H OLED.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: RGB LED is the newest premium LCD approach but still trails OLED on black levels, so the two technologies will keep splitting the high end of the TV market.
insights.quote: So you have to pick your poison.

insights.claim: Sony (Bravia 9 II, branded "True RGB"), LG (Micro RGB Evo) and Samsung (Micro RGB R95H) all sell RGB-panel TVs. In Wired's testing the LG Micro RGB Evo was slightly more colorful than the Sony.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: RGB LED is now a product category across all three big TV brands, which is worth tracking as a new front in the premium-panel competition.
insights.locator: The current flagship television from Sony

insights.claim: The Sony Bravia 9 II's main draw is a very bright RGB panel with no glare and some of the widest viewing angles Wired has tested. Users can set the black level by hand (the reviewer used 61 out of 100) to rescue dark films, but this takes time.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: The appeal is for enthusiasts who like to tweak. The product depends on user calibration rather than out-of-the-box picture quality.
insights.quote: Knowing you can achieve those results is nice; actually doing it does take time.

insights.claim: Only two of the Sony Bravia 9 II's four HDMI ports are HDMI 2.1 (48 Gbps). Through those ports, gaming latency at 120 Hz was almost nonexistent.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Limited HDMI 2.1 ports are a recurring trade-off in premium TVs that matters to buyers with several consoles.
insights.locator: The Sony Bravia 9 II is all black

insights.claim: Google TV on the Sony Bravia 9 II took under five minutes to set up. Samsung TVs add a login authentication step and LG TVs rely on the LG ThinQ app. The Sony remote has a center button for the Google Gemini voice assistant.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Google's TV OS and Gemini assistant are spreading on third-party TVs, while Samsung and LG keep their own ecosystems.
insights.locator: The Sony Bravia 9 II is all black

insights.claim: The Bravia 9 II has two upfiring tweeters for Dolby Atmos that the midrange Bravia 7 II lacks. Sony uses audio channels as well as brightness to separate its flagship from its midrange model.
insights.speaker: John Brandon
insights.so_what: Sony's feature segmentation between its flagship and midrange models suggests how it defends premium pricing.
